lessons.title: Docker Mental Model
lessons.why: Here’s the simple reason this matters: An image is an immutable filesystem/runtime template; a container is a running isolated process created from that image. Containers still use ordinary processes, files, ports, and networks. In this course, we connect it directly to containers, CI/CD, Vercel, production release, smoke testing, and rollback, so you can see where the idea lives in a real project instead of memorizing a definition.
objectives: Explain Docker Mental Model in terms of inputs, owner, outputs, and failure modes.
Implement Docker Mental Model incrementally and predict observable evidence before execution.
Diagnose a controlled Docker Mental Model failure from evidence.
Apply Docker Mental Model to a new TaskFlow requirement without copying the reference implementation.

mentalModel: Start with the plain-English idea. An image is an immutable filesystem/runtime template; a container is a running isolated process created from that image. Containers still use ordinary processes, files, ports, and networks.

Now place it in TaskFlow. This lesson belongs to containers, CI/CD, Vercel, production release, smoke testing, and rollback. Ask four questions while you work: what enters this boundary, who owns the decision, what dependency does it use, and what evidence proves the result?

Keep the change small. Predict what you should see before you run anything, then compare the prediction with the real terminal, browser, HTTP, database, test, container, or CI evidence. If they differ, debug the first mismatch instead of editing several places at random.
The goal is not to remember the exact snippet below. The goal is to be able to explain Docker Mental Model in your own words, rebuild the core behavior, and adapt it when the requirement changes.
